2026-09-21-stratasys-bambu-verdict.artAlt: Dithered photograph: 3D printer nozzle extruding plastic (15425525988).
2026-09-21-stratasys-bambu-verdict.artCredit: Photo: David Elliott from UK — CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
2026-09-21-stratasys-bambu-verdict.author: Desk
2026-09-21-stratasys-bambu-verdict.body:
A federal jury in the Eastern District of Texas found four @BambuLab-related companies liable for infringing four @Stratasys patents, and awarded $27.6m in damages. The verdict came on 17 September after a week-long trial.

WHAT THE PATENTS COVER

Two of them, US 9,168,698 and US 10,556,381, cover force detection during fabrication — the mechanism behind automatic bed levelling. US 9,421,713 covers purge towers, the sacrificial block a multi-material printer wipes its nozzle into between colours. US 7,555,357 covers extrusion-based layered deposition systems generally.

The jury found all four valid and infringed by the @BambuLabX1, @BambuLabP1 and @BambuLabA1 lines. It also found the infringement wilful, which is what opens the door to enhanced damages later.

WHAT HAS NOT HAPPENED

No injunction has been issued. @BambuLab's printers remain on sale, and @BambuLab disputes the verdict. This was the first of two patent cases @Stratasys filed against @BambuLab in the same court; the second has not been tried.

WHY IT MATTERS

Purge towers and automatic bed levelling are not @BambuLab-specific tricks — they are how a consumer multi-material printer works, across brands. A wilfulness finding on patents that broad, in the court that hears the most patent cases in America, is a bill that other desktop printer makers should read carefully.

Source: Tom's Hardware, 21 September 2026, on the 17 September jury verdict in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Texas.
2026-09-21-stratasys-bambu-verdict.deck: $27.6m in damages, four patents covering purge towers and force-detection bed levelling, and no injunction — the printers stay on sale. This was the first of two trials.
2026-09-21-stratasys-bambu-verdict.headline: A Texas jury says @BambuLab's X1, P1 and A1 infringe four @Stratasys patents, and did it wilfully

2026-09-21-zai-zcode-workspace-upload.artCredit: Photo: Unknown — CC0, via Wikimedia Commons
2026-09-21-zai-zcode-workspace-upload.author: Desk
2026-09-21-zai-zcode-workspace-upload.body:
A developer publishing as @Ferstar found that @ZCode, the coding tool from Beijing's @ZAI — the company behind the @GLM models — was silently packaging their local workspace and uploading it. The snapshot ran to 313MB of a commercial project, git history and all, bound for cloud storage. The upload failed and retried 564 times.

THE PART THAT IS WORSE THAN THE UPLOAD

The archive is encrypted, and the private key sits on @ZAI's back end. @Ferstar could not open it. Neither could the @ZCode client on their own machine. So the only party who can say what was in that archive is the party that took it — and the same goes for @ZAI's assurance that the data has since been destroyed. There is no way for an outsider to check either claim.

The upload was on by default, and there was no setting to turn it off.

WHAT @ZAI SAYS

@ZAI apologised on Friday, said it has fixed the uploading of user files without consent, and says data already sent to its cloud has been deleted. It has also open-sourced @ZCode, which at least lets people read the code that did this.

WHY IT MATTERS

Coding agents run where the source lives. The trust they need is not "will you write good code" but "will you leave the repository where you found it". A default-on snapshot with no opt-out and a vendor-held key fails that test in the most literal way available — and open-sourcing the client afterwards does not retrieve anything already sent.

Source: Tom's Hardware, 21 September 2026, with the original finding published by the developer Ferstar.

2026-09-21-zai-zcode-workspace-upload.headline: @ZAI's coding tool packed up a developer's whole workspace, encrypted it with a key only @ZAI holds, and tried 564 times to send it

2026-09-21-windows-seven-hour-update.artAlt: Dithered photograph: A One Laptop per Child computer Keyboard (1273773764).
2026-09-21-windows-seven-hour-update.artCredit: Photo: Simon Law from Montréal, QC, Canada — CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
2026-09-21-windows-seven-hour-update.author: Desk
2026-09-21-windows-seven-hour-update.body:
WHAT WAS TESTED
A journalist at @TheRegister took a @Windows11 laptop that had last been fully up to date less than a year ago, started the update process, and timed how long it took to get current. The answer was about seven hours, reported on 20 September.

WHAT SEVEN HOURS CONSISTS OF
Not one download. A large set of updates to @Windows components, several firmware updates, several driver updates, and repeated restarts, each of which re-enters the queue rather than finishing it. The write-up reserves particular contempt for the interface during all this — "a progress bar of lies and the percentage counter of deceit".

WHY THIS IS NOT JUST A COMPLAINT
The interesting number is the gap. This was not a decade-old machine; it was current within the year. Servicing that assumes a device checks in continuously degrades sharply for a device that does not, and the cost lands on exactly the machines least able to absorb it: spares, loaners, lab boxes, the laptop in the drawer that someone needs working this afternoon.

WHAT IS NOT HERE
This is one reporter's machine, timed once, not a benchmark across a fleet, and there is no @Microsoft response in the piece. Treat it as an account of an experience rather than a measurement.

Source: @TheRegister, "How Windows turned months of inactivity into a 7-hour update hostage situation", 20 September 2026.
2026-09-21-windows-seven-hour-update.deck: @TheRegister put a machine that had been left alone through the update process and timed it. Components, firmware, drivers, restarts — and a progress bar it describes as lying.
2026-09-21-windows-seven-hour-update.headline: A @Windows11 laptop that was current less than a year ago took about seven hours to catch up

2026-09-21-crusoe-series-f-30-9bn.artAlt: Dithered photograph: CSX Intermodal container with truck and trailer, Denver, CO 2021-03-24.
2026-09-21-crusoe-series-f-30-9bn.artCredit: Photo: Xnatedawgx — CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
2026-09-21-crusoe-series-f-30-9bn.author: Desk
2026-09-21-crusoe-series-f-30-9bn.body:
THE ROUND
@Crusoe raised $3.9bn in a Series F that values it at $30.9bn, the company announced and @TechCrunch reported on 17 September. It was co-led by @AtreidesManagement, @MubadalaCapital and @ValorEquityPartners, with @FoundersFund, @GIC, @NVIDIA, the @QatarInvestmentAuthority, @RadicalVentures and @TPG also taking part.

THE REPRICING
The comparison is the interesting part. Ten months earlier, last October, @Crusoe raised $1.38bn at a $10bn valuation. Roughly a 3x mark in under a year, with an accelerator maker on the cap table.

WHAT THE MONEY BUILDS
Two different things. The first is conventional: financing existing projects, including the large @Abilene, Texas site used by @OpenAI. The second is @Spark — smaller modular AI factories manufactured in @Crusoe's own facilities and moved by truck. The stated advantage is deployment speed without assembling a large construction workforce on site, which is the binding constraint on most of this build-out.

WHERE THE COMPANY CAME FROM
@Crusoe was founded in 2018 as a crypto mining operation running on flared natural gas, and turned to AI infrastructure as demand for compute rose. Its customers include @Meta, @Microsoft and @Oracle.

Source: @TechCrunch, "Crusoe raises $3.9B to build massive data centers and small modular 'AI factories'", 17 September 2026.
2026-09-21-crusoe-series-f-30-9bn.deck: Ten months ago the round was $1.38bn at $10bn. @NVIDIA is in this one. The money funds the @OpenAI site at Abilene and @Spark, a modular AI factory built in @Crusoe's own plants so a deployment does not need a construction workforce.
2026-09-21-crusoe-series-f-30-9bn.headline: @Crusoe raises $3.9bn at $30.9bn, and part of it goes on data centres that arrive on a truck

2026-09-21-rtx-60-slips-to-2028.artAlt: Dithered photograph: Club3D S3 Deltachrome S8 card with cooler.
2026-09-21-rtx-60-slips-to-2028.artCredit: Photo: Mentalist — CC0, via Wikimedia Commons
2026-09-21-rtx-60-slips-to-2028.author: Desk
2026-09-21-rtx-60-slips-to-2028.body:
WHAT IS CLAIMED
@kopite7kimi, a hardware leaker with a long and unusually good track record, posted that @NVIDIA's @RTX60 series — consumer parts built on the @Rubin architecture — will not arrive until at least 2028. "Unfortunately, GR20x is a product from 2028. That means they have postponed again," the post read. @TomsHardware carried it on 21 September, and @VideoCardz reported a second leaker reaching the same conclusion.

MARK THIS AS RUMOUR
This is a leak, not an @NVIDIA statement. There is no product page, no roadmap slide and no company comment. The same leaker previously expected the generation in the second half of 2027, which is the point: the claim being made is that a date moved, and the previous date was also a leak.

THE STATED REASON
The explanation attached to it is priority, not capability. @NVIDIA had originally aimed @RTX60 at 2026, pushed it to 2027 so that AI accelerator demand could absorb more @TSMC capacity, and is now said to have pushed it again. A structural GDDR7 shortage is cited as compounding it.

WHAT IT WOULD MEAN
If it holds, the @RTX50 generation carries consumer graphics for an unusually long stretch, and the refresh parts stop being a stopgap and become the line. Set against the memory pricing story running this week, a long gap between generations and a tight DRAM market point the same way on street prices.

Source: @TomsHardware, "Nvidia's next-gen RTX 60 GPUs might not be released until 2028, prominent leaker claims", 21 September 2026.
2026-09-21-rtx-60-slips-to-2028.deck: RUMOUR. @kopite7kimi now puts the Rubin-based consumer parts in 2028, having previously expected late 2027. The reading is that gaming silicon keeps losing the argument to the data centre.
2026-09-21-rtx-60-slips-to-2028.headline: @NVIDIA's @RTX60 has slipped again, to 2028, according to the leaker who called the last delay

2026-09-21-acer-memory-price-signalling.artCredit: Photo: User Kotepho on en.wikipedia — Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
2026-09-21-acer-memory-price-signalling.author: Desk
2026-09-21-acer-memory-price-signalling.body:
WHAT HE SAID
@Acer chairman @JasonChen told reporters that repeated claims from the top three memory suppliers — @Samsung, @SKhynix and @Micron — that price increases will run until 2027 are not statements of fact but a way for the three to signal one another in public, because antitrust rules stop them talking directly. @TomsHardware reported the remarks on 21 September.

THE MARGIN ARGUMENT
His reading is that the three want to keep gross margins "in the 80% range for as long as possible", which is why they keep publicly asserting that nothing will get cheaper before a given year. On the forecast of a shortage running to 2030, he was blunt: "A shortage until 2030 is impossible."

WHAT HE SAYS THE SUPPLY ACTUALLY LOOKS LIKE
@JasonChen's account is that memory is no longer genuinely short — warehouses are full, there are many sellers and few buyers — and that cheaper Chinese capacity coming online is disruptive to pricing.

WHAT IT MEANS FOR A PC
He is not promising relief now. His own forecast has PC prices rising another 5% to 20% towards the end of this year, plateauing through the first half of 2027, and only then declining.

WHOSE INTEREST IS WHOSE
Worth holding both halves. @Acer buys memory; a chairman arguing in public that his suppliers are talking their own book is himself talking his own book. What is checkable is the forecast, and it carries a date.

Source: @TomsHardware, "Acer CEO says memory makers are hyping 2030 shortage fears to protect margins", 21 September 2026.
2026-09-21-acer-memory-price-signalling.deck: @JasonChen says warehouses are full and a shortage lasting to 2030 is impossible. He reads @Samsung, @SKhynix and @Micron's public "prices will keep rising" statements as signalling under antitrust rules, aimed at holding gross margins in the 80s.
2026-09-21-acer-memory-price-signalling.headline: @Acer's chairman says the memory shortage talk is the three suppliers calling the roll to each other

2026-09-21-saturn-ai-financial-advice.artCredit: Photo: Ancelli — CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
2026-09-21-saturn-ai-financial-advice.author: Desk
2026-09-21-saturn-ai-financial-advice.body:
WHAT WAS TESTED
UK fintech firm @Saturn published "Artificial Authority: Should you trust AI to deliver financial advice?", running 121 personal finance questions through 18 free and paid AI models — among them @ChatGPT, @Claude, @Gemini, @Copilot and @Grok. Each question was asked up to five times to check consistency, producing more than 10,000 answers.

THE HEADLINE NUMBER
57% of answers were inaccurate. On complex questions the average error rate rose to 88%, and some models failed as many as 99% of the hardest ones.

PAID BEATS FREE, BUT NOT BY MUCH
Free models failed 63% of answers against 49% for paid versions. @ClaudeOpus5 in reasoning mode led the field — and still failed 39%.

WHAT WENT WRONG
The report groups the failures rather than treating them as one fault: calculation errors, omitted risk warnings, answers that did not account for upcoming tax changes, and financial rules that were stated confidently and do not exist. @Saturn's framing is that the errors could cost users "tens of thousands of pounds".

WHY THE SHAPE MATTERS
A flat 57% would be a quality problem. An error rate that climbs from the average to 88% as the question gets harder is a different problem: the model is least reliable exactly where a person is least able to check it.

Source: @ProfessionalAdviser, "AI models give inaccurate financial advice 57% of the time", 14 September 2026, reporting @Saturn's study. Picked up more widely this week.
2026-09-21-saturn-ai-financial-advice.deck: @Saturn's test put the same personal finance questions through @ChatGPT, @Claude, @Gemini, @Copilot and @Grok five times each. On the hardest questions the average error rate was 88%, and some models missed 99%.
2026-09-21-saturn-ai-financial-advice.headline: 18 AI models were asked 121 money questions 10,000 times, and got 57% of the answers wrong

2026-09-21-samsung-hbm4-double.artCredit: Photo: Peellden — CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
2026-09-21-samsung-hbm4-double.author: Desk
2026-09-21-samsung-hbm4-double.body:
WHAT WAS REPORTED
@Samsung is expected to more than double output of its @HBM4 family — sixth-generation @HBM4 and seventh-generation @HBM4E — next year, @SeoulEconomicDaily reported on 20 September, citing semiconductor industry sources. Total @Samsung HBM production is expected to grow by almost 40%, from roughly 180,000 wafers a month this year to about 250,000 next year. Within that total, the @HBM4 family's share rises from about 40% to about 80%.

THE GLASS CARRIER NUMBER
The supporting figure is a consumable, not a chip. Glass carriers, used in @HBM4 packaging, were running at 10,000 sheets a month last year and 20,000 this year. @Samsung is reported to be raising outsourced cleaning volume to 50,000 sheets a month next year — a 2.5-fold increase. Consumables and cleaning contracts are booked before wafers move, which is why they read as a forward signal.

WHERE THE PARTS ALREADY ARE
@Samsung began mass-production shipments of @HBM4 in February, on 10nm-class sixth-generation (1c) DRAM with a base die built on a 4nm process. In May it supplied 12-layer @HBM4E samples to customers including @NVIDIA.

WHAT AN INDUSTRY OFFICIAL SAID
"As @Samsung expands HBM production, it appears to be placing @HBM4, a high-value product, at the center," an industry official told the paper.

THE CAVEAT
This is a sourced report, not a @Samsung announcement. The wafer and sheet figures come from industry sources and suppliers rather than from the company, and @Samsung has not confirmed them.

Source: @SeoulEconomicDaily, "Samsung to Double HBM4 Output Next Year, Sources Say", 20 September 2026.
2026-09-21-samsung-hbm4-double.deck: Monthly HBM wafers go from about 180,000 to about 250,000. The @HBM4 family goes from roughly 40% of that to roughly 80%. The number that gave it away was glass carriers: 20,000 sheets a month now, 50,000 next year.
2026-09-21-samsung-hbm4-double.headline: @Samsung will more than double its @HBM4 output next year, and the tell is a glass-cleaning contract

2026-09-21-cambium-cnmaestro-off.artCredit: Photo: Unknown — CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
2026-09-21-cambium-cnmaestro-off.author: Desk
2026-09-21-cambium-cnmaestro-off.body:
WHAT IS BEING TURNED OFF
@CambiumNetworks, which is in administration, ends @cnMaestroCloud for enterprise devices on 1 October, @TheRegister reported on 21 September. Customers have to install the on-premises version of @cnMaestro before that date or lose cloud management of their hardware.

THE CATCH AFTER THE CATCH
The on-premises trial licence runs for 90 days from migration. After it expires the software drops to reduced functionality. @Cambium's wording on what comes next is a hope rather than a plan: "We expect that if the Enterprise business is acquired by an entity, they will help you with an appropriate extension or replacement."

WHAT ELSE IS GOING
The whole enterprise line is being discontinued alongside the portal — Wi-Fi access points, @NSE firewalls and @cnMatrix switches.

THE STATE OF THE COMPANY
260 staff, 53.6% of the workforce, were laid off without severance. @Nasdaq delisted the company after financial reporting irregularities, with its 2022 and 2023 reports deemed unreliable. In May 2026 executives acknowledged "substantial doubt about our ability to continue as a going concern."

WHAT SURVIVES
The fixed wireless broadband business is expected to resume after a brief pause. That is the part of @Cambium with a future attached; the enterprise networking customers are the ones with ten days.

Source: @TheRegister, 21 September 2026 — https://www.theregister.com/networks/2026/09/21/failed-networking-vendor-cambium-set-to-turn-off-its-cloudy-management-portal/5297647
2026-09-21-cambium-cnmaestro-off.deck: The on-premises replacement comes with a 90-day trial licence and no committed plan for what follows it. @Cambium's own word for what happens next is “expect”.
2026-09-21-cambium-cnmaestro-off.headline: @Cambium switches off @cnMaestroCloud on 1 October, giving customers ten days to move their kit

2026-09-21-salesforce-outcome-pricing.artCredit: Photo: Swtpc6800 Michael Holley — Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
2026-09-21-salesforce-outcome-pricing.author: Desk
2026-09-21-salesforce-outcome-pricing.body:
WHAT IS BEING TRIED
@Salesforce is moving off pure per-seat licensing for its AI products, in particular the newly unveiled @AIforce platform, @TheRegister reported on 21 September. Three approaches are running at the same time: conventional seat licences, consumption-based @FlexCredits that customers refill, and outcome-based pricing — an AI customer service agent billed by the number of cases it resolves.

THE QUOTE THE COMPANY DID NOT NEED
"An anxiety-filled architecture right now of different pricing structures" is how deputy CFO @MikeSpencer described where things stand. @BillPatterson, executive VP for CRM applications, put the same thing forward as "a new pricing structure that really aligns to the benefits that customers realize."

THE OTHER TWO SHAPES
Beside those sit @AgenticEnterpriseLicenseAgreements — a fixed price for broad access — and @SalesforceCommit, a spending commitment the customer allocates as it likes, the example given being $10m over three years.

HOW LONG THIS TAKES
@Spencer expects consumption revenue to become material within three to five years. @PreetTakkar, @PwC's global @Salesforce leader, expects outcome-based pricing to be far more prevalent by 2030. Both are forecasts, not results, and neither company has published what share of revenue the new models carry today.

THE BACKDROP
A seven-hour global outage during @Dreamforce 2026 sits behind the conversation, and it is a reminder that what is being repriced is something customers already cannot work without.

Source: @TheRegister, 21 September 2026 — https://www.theregister.com/software/2026/09/21/salesforce-wants-to-charge-for-ai-outcomes-but-first-it-needs-to-figure-out-how/5297402
2026-09-21-salesforce-outcome-pricing.deck: Seat licences, refillable @FlexCredits and outcome pricing are all running at once on @AIforce. An AI service agent billed per case resolved is the shape the company says it is aiming at.
2026-09-21-salesforce-outcome-pricing.headline: @Salesforce wants to bill for AI results, and its own deputy CFO calls the pricing “anxiety-filled”

2026-09-21-toyota-eley-400k.artAlt: Dithered photograph: Robotic Arm Polishing Guitars at Martin Guitar Factory.
2026-09-21-toyota-eley-400k.artCredit: Photo: Henrysz — CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
2026-09-21-toyota-eley-400k.author: Desk
2026-09-21-toyota-eley-400k.body:
WHAT WAS ANNOUNCED
@Toyota plans to deploy roughly 400,000 robots across its own plants and those of its group companies from 2028, @AutomotiveWorld reported on 18 September. About 150,000 go into @Toyota's own factories and 250,000 across group company sites, spanning some 60 plants worldwide. The spending figure attached to it is around ¥1 trillion (about $6.4bn) a year from 2028 — that is factory renewal in total, not robots alone.

THE ROBOT
@Eley stands for Embodied Learning robot for Enhanced Yield. It is a 50kg wheeled platform, not a bipedal humanoid, and it has two-fingered grippers rather than anthropomorphic hands. It runs on battery or a direct cord.

HOW IT LEARNS
Workers wear finger-shaped jigs modelled on the robot's hands while doing routine tasks, so @Eley learns the technique from demonstration rather than from simulation or bought-in datasets. At a technology briefing at @Toyota's European headquarters earlier in September it folded T-shirts with near-perfect accuracy after 1,500 practice sessions over about two weeks. @Toyota says the expertise of 18,000 veteran takumi workers becomes the training data.

WHAT TOYOTA SAYS IT IS FOR
"We aim for a world where robots coexist with humans, rather than replacing them," said executive vice president @HirokiNakajima. The stated division of labour is robots on repetitive and physically demanding work, people on the judgement calls that still need a trained eye.

WHAT IS NOT CONFIRMED
The 400,000 figure is a plan from 2028 onwards, not an order book. No per-unit cost has been published, and @Toyota has not said which of the 60 plants take robots first.

Source: @AutomotiveWorld, 18 September 2026 — https://www.automotiveworld.com/news/toyota-plans-to-deploy-400000-factory-robots-from-2028/
2026-09-21-toyota-eley-400k.deck: From 2028, about ¥1 trillion a year and roughly 400,000 robots across 60 plants. @Eley is not a walking humanoid — it is a 50kg wheeled platform with two fingers that learns by watching people.
2026-09-21-toyota-eley-400k.headline: @Toyota plans 400,000 @Eley robots in its factories, trained on 18,000 veteran workers

2026-09-21-upi-merchant-fee.artAlt: Dithered photograph: Credit card terminal in Laos.
2026-09-21-upi-merchant-fee.artCredit: Photo: Basile Morin — CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
2026-09-21-upi-merchant-fee.author: Desk
2026-09-21-upi-merchant-fee.body:
WHAT CHANGES
From 15 October a 0.4% merchant discount rate applies to @UPI payments made to businesses above ₹2,000 (about $21), capped at ₹300 per transaction, @AlJazeera reported on 17 September. Service categories — fuel, railway tickets, telecom bills — pay a flat ₹5 instead. Person-to-person transfers stay free, and so does any merchant payment at or below ₹2,000.

THE SCALE OF WHAT IS BEING CHARGED FOR
@UPI processed 24.51 billion transactions last month, about 791 million a day, worth more than $10bn a day. Over a year that is 241.6 billion transactions worth close to $3.3 trillion, which @AlJazeera puts at roughly half of all real-time digital payments in the world.

WHO COLLECTS
The estimated ₹170bn annual revenue pool splits about 60% to banks, 25% to app providers and 15% to aggregators. @Paytm, @AxisBank and @YesBank gained between 2% and 8% after the announcement.

WHO OBJECTS
The @RetailersAssociationOfIndia warns that small merchants will reconsider accepting @UPI at all. @Congress spokesperson @JairamRamesh called the move a capitulation to "US pressure", arguing it makes room for American payment companies to compete with India's own system.

WHAT NPCI SAYS IT COSTS
@NPCI's case is operating cost: running @UPI, its server bandwidth, fraud prevention and the technical support banks need, is put at roughly ₹20,000 crore a year.

Source: @AlJazeera, 17 September 2026 — https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2026/9/17/india-to-impose-controversial-fee-for-upi-instant-payments-who-benefits
2026-09-21-upi-merchant-fee.deck: Person-to-person stays free, and so does anything at or under ₹2,000. Everything else that a shop takes now carries a cut, on a system running 791 million payments a day.
2026-09-21-upi-merchant-fee.headline: India's free instant payments end on 15 October: 0.4% on merchant @UPI above ₹2,000

2026-09-21-vmware-smartnic-retreat.artCredit: Photo: CEphoto, Uwe Aranas — CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
2026-09-21-vmware-smartnic-retreat.author: Desk
2026-09-21-vmware-smartnic-retreat.body:
WHAT CHANGED
@VMware has discontinued sales of its distributed firewall for SmartNICs, @TheRegister reported on 21 September. The @DistributedServicesEngine — the product built to run @VMware software on the data processing units inside those cards — remains supported within @VMwareCloudFoundation, but no longer gets active development for SmartNIC deployment.

THE PITCH THAT DID NOT LAND
The idea was to take a hyperscaler pattern, offloading networking and security onto the network card's own processor, and bring it into the on-premises private cloud. @VMware ported its products to @AMD and @Nvidia SmartNICs successfully. @Intel hardware proved harder, which @TheRegister puts down to microcode complexity.

WHY IT STOPPED
"Customers kept talking, but not buying," said @UmeshMahajan, VP and GM of @Broadcom's application networking division. The other half of the answer is that conventional network interface cards evolved a long way, which narrowed the advantage SmartNICs were sold on in the first place.

WHAT SURVIVES
@VMware is still working on acceleration by other routes, including direct offload using @Nvidia's @ConnectX7, alongside memory tiering, global deduplication and its AI Factory work. Because most SmartNIC processors are Arm parts, the underlying engineering may resurface in @VMware's Arm-based @ESX hypervisor.

Source: @TheRegister, 21 September 2026 — https://www.theregister.com/virtualization/2026/09/21/vmware-has-quietly-walked-back-its-smartnic-ambitions/5297654
2026-09-21-vmware-smartnic-retreat.deck: The @DistributedServicesEngine is still supported inside @VMwareCloudFoundation, but is no longer actively developed for SmartNIC deployment. Ordinary network cards got good enough.
2026-09-21-vmware-smartnic-retreat.headline: @VMware has stopped selling its SmartNIC firewall: “Customers kept talking, but not buying”

2026-09-21-world-model-secrecy.artAlt: Dithered photograph: A student using a Theodolite in field.
2026-09-21-world-model-secrecy.artCredit: Photo: Kskhh — CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
2026-09-21-world-model-secrecy.author: Desk
2026-09-21-world-model-secrecy.body:
WHAT THE REPORTING FOUND
@AMILabs, founded by @YannLeCun, and @WorldLabs, founded by @FeiFeiLi, are among the best-funded companies working on world models, and neither will discuss commercial plans or timelines, @TechCrunch's @RussellBrandom reported on 20 September. "We'll talk about it when we're ready to talk about it," said @AMILabs co-founder @MichaelRabbat. By email he added that the company is "still in a research and building phase, so we're not talking publicly about any product plans or timeline."

WHAT A WORLD MODEL IS FOR
The field is about automating spatial intelligence, with applications named in robotics, video games, CGI effects, self-driving and manufacturing. @Waymo, @OpenAI and @Anthropic are all named as companies that could move onto the same ground.

WHO PAYS FOR THE SILENCE
The cost lands further down the chain. "I wish they would tell us more. We could build more useful data if we knew what they were working on," said @AlexdeVigan, chief executive of the data supplier @Physicl.

WHY STAY QUIET
@Brandom's reading is a dark forest: saying nothing delays a competitor's response, and a few months of delay is worth more than the attention a launch would buy.

THIS IS AN ABSENCE, NOT A DISCLOSURE
No product, price or date was announced by any of these companies. The story is that there is nothing to announce yet, and that this is now deliberate.

Source: @TechCrunch, 20 September 2026 — https://techcrunch.com/2026/09/20/world-model-companies-are-keeping-a-lot-of-secrets/
2026-09-21-world-model-secrecy.deck: @AMILabs and @WorldLabs have money, founders and research, and no public product plan. The data companies downstream say the silence is costing them work.
2026-09-21-world-model-secrecy.headline: The best-funded world model companies will not say what they are building, and their suppliers are guessing

2026-09-21-anderon-quantum-foundry.body:
WHAT WAS SIGNED
@Anderon, an @IBM company, has finalised a $1bn award from the @DepartmentOfCommerce under the @CHIPSAct. The money supports research and development for quantum wafer manufacturing at @Anderon's 300-millimetre pure-play quantum wafer foundry at the @AlbanyNanoTech Complex in Albany, New York. @IBM is putting in an additional $1bn of its own.

FINALISED, NOT PROPOSED
The distinction matters. The $1bn was announced as a proposed award in May 2026, when @IBM and the @DepartmentOfCommerce presented it as America's first purpose-built quantum foundry. September's news is that the agreement is now signed.

WHAT IT MAKES TODAY
The fab is operating and has begun running its first quantum wafers. Current output is superconducting qubit arrays plus the quantum input/output signalling and readout chain that goes with them. The roadmap extends the same 300mm line past superconducting processors into silicon photonics and spin-qubit devices.

WHAT THEY SAID
"This agreement with the Department of Commerce strengthens our ability to deliver the manufacturing scale the quantum industry needs," said @MukeshKhare, chief executive of @Anderon.

@JayGambetta, director of @IBMResearch and an @IBM Fellow, framed it as a division of labour: "Anderon's focus on wafer fabrication gives us exactly that and strengthens our ability to execute and accelerate progress."

THE PART TO WATCH
A pure-play foundry only means something if somebody other than the parent buys from it. @Anderon's entire current product line is @IBM's own modality. Whether the silicon photonics and spin-qubit expansion arrives with outside customers attached is the test of the "pure-play" word.

Source: @TheQuantumInsider, "Anderon Finalizes $1 Billion CHIPS Award for Quantum Wafer Manufacturing", 16 September 2026. @DIGITIMES carried the story on 21 September.

2026-09-21-delft-whisker-drone.artCredit: Photo: U.S. Air Force photo by Senior Airman Karalyn Degraffenreed — Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
2026-09-21-delft-whisker-drone.author: Desk
2026-09-21-delft-whisker-drone.body:
THE WORK
Researchers at @TUDelft have built a whisker-based tactile sensor light enough for a drone under 100 grams, and shown it navigating with no camera, no rangefinder and no light. The paper is in @NatureCommunications, published 18 September 2026, DOI 10.1038/s41467-026-77366-7, by @ChaoxiangYe, @GuidodeCroon and @SaluaHamaza.

HOW IT WORKS
A pair of artificial whiskers is mounted at the front of the airframe. Each one has three miniature pressure sensors at its base. When the whisker bends against a surface, the pattern of pressure change is used to estimate where the contact happened in three dimensions and how deep it went. The idea is copied from rodent vibrissae.

THE NUMBER THAT MATTERS
The tactile perception pipeline uses about 34 kilobytes of RAM and runs entirely onboard, in real time, on a microcontroller. That is the whole point: sub-100-gram robots cannot carry a camera, a processor big enough to use it, and the battery for both.

WHAT THEY FLEW
The team demonstrated following rigid and soft surface contours in complete darkness, wall-following to explore an enclosed space, building a tactile map of an unfamiliar room, and finding the way out of it without any vision sensor. Transparent walls — the case that defeats most optical sensing — were among the surfaces.

"We wanted to show that touch does not have to come at the cost of size or computational power," said @ChaoxiangYe.

ONE FIGURE TO BE CAREFUL WITH
@TUDelft's own release describes the depth estimates as millimetre-precision. @TomsHardware headlined the same work as "sub-millimetre". Those are not the same claim, and the release is the one to go by.

Source: @TUDelft press release via @EurekAlert, "Bio-inspired whiskers enable tiny drones to navigate in darkness using touch", 18 September 2026.
2026-09-21-delft-whisker-drone.deck: @TUDelft put a pair of artificial whiskers on the front of a palm-sized drone and flew it along walls in total darkness. The whole tactile pipeline fits in 34 kilobytes.
2026-09-21-delft-whisker-drone.headline: A 100-gram drone that flies by touch, using whiskers and 34KB of RAM

2026-09-21-npm-btree-runtime-malware.artAlt: Dithered photograph: EFTA00002419 - Cluttered server rack filled with tangled cables and equipment in a dimly lit room.
2026-09-21-npm-btree-runtime-malware.artCredit: Photo: Federal Bureau of Investigation — Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
2026-09-21-npm-btree-runtime-malware.author: Desk
2026-09-21-npm-btree-runtime-malware.body:
WHAT WAS FOUND
@Checkmarx researchers identified ten malicious @npm packages that carry no malicious install script at all. The loader sits inside the library's own BTree.prototype.set method and fires at runtime, when an application calls it with a particular key value.

WHY THAT DEFEATS THE DEFENCE
@GitHub tightened @npm in June 2026, and @npm v12 makes install scripts go through an approval step. That control only sees installation. "The malware loader hides inside the library's own BTree.prototype.set method, which is the main function that every user would call constantly," @Checkmarx said. Installing the package looks entirely clean.

THE PACKAGES
indexed-btree, at about 2 million weekly downloads, and btree-core, at 1,951,274, are the two big ones. The rest: ordered-kv-index (448,184), btree-leaderboard (493,685), priority-slot-queue (402,860), btree-range-store (468,092), btree-time-index (425,312), btree-lru-cache (372,185), neighbor-key-map (366,019) and sliding-score-window (448,024).

WHAT IT DOES ONCE RUNNING
Collects architecture, hostname, CPU, memory and uptime. Exfiltrates through hardcoded @Slack and @Telegram channels. Polls an @Ethereum smart contract on the Sepolia test network for command-and-control details. Uses X25519 key exchange to derive AES keys and decrypt a second stage. It can delete files and remove its own triggers afterwards.

THE CREDIBILITY TRICK
The authors built legitimate-looking @GitHub repositories with fabricated commit histories behind each package. @Checkmarx notes a wallet holding 109 ETH tied to the operation, but does not claim those funds came from theft.

WHAT TO DO
@Checkmarx's advice is runtime behavioural analysis rather than install-time scanning alone. Anyone who installed one of the ten should rotate every secret and rebuild the development environment from a known-good backup.

Source: @BleepingComputer, "Malicious npm packages evade install-script defenses at runtime", 20 September 2026.
2026-09-21-npm-btree-runtime-malware.deck: @Checkmarx found the loader inside BTree.prototype.set. Installation looks clean, so @npm v12's approval step never fires. One of the packages had 2 million weekly downloads.
2026-09-21-npm-btree-runtime-malware.headline: Ten @npm packages hid their malware in a function every user calls, sidestepping install-script scanning

2026-09-21-rathat-ai-android.artCredit: Photo: Mbrickn — CC0, via Wikimedia Commons
2026-09-21-rathat-ai-android.author: Desk
2026-09-21-rathat-ai-android.body:
WHAT IT IS
@Zimperium's zLabs researchers have described @RatHat, an Android remote-access trojan with an AI subsystem that handles on-screen navigation. It spreads through malvertising, SMS and phishing pages pushing APK downloads from outside @GooglePlay.

THE MECHANISM
@RatHat serialises the Android Accessibility tree into XML and sends it to a popular AI assistant, which @Zimperium does not name. The assistant returns the coordinates of interface elements, reads the on-screen text, and hands back navigation instructions — "SCROLL_DOWN" and the like. The malware then acts on them.

WHY THAT IS DIFFERENT
"RatHat uses AI to intelligently navigate and control the device interface in real-time, making its operations more adaptable and harder for security software to detect than traditional, scripted automation," @Zimperium said. Detection that looks for a fixed sequence of taps has nothing to match against.

THE REST OF THE KIT
It enables Developer Options and Wireless Debugging to get shell-level execution, installs Go-based agents for command execution and persistence, captures credentials through HTML overlays on banking and cryptocurrency apps, intercepts SMS and one-time passwords, logs keystrokes and lock-screen PINs, and keeps a tunnel open with an FRP reverse proxy.

WHO
@Zimperium links it to Chinese threat actors, on the basis that the prompts sent to the AI assistant are written in Chinese. That is an inference from artefacts, not an identification.

Source: @BleepingComputer, "New RatHat Android malware uses AI to automate device control", 17 September 2026.
2026-09-21-rathat-ai-android.deck: @Zimperium found Android malware that serialises the screen to XML, asks a commercial AI assistant what to tap, and gets back instructions. The prompts are written in Chinese.
2026-09-21-rathat-ai-android.headline: @RatHat feeds the Android accessibility tree to an AI assistant and lets it drive the phone

2026-09-21-waterplum-fake-interviews.artCredit: Photo: Federal Bureau of Investigation — Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
2026-09-21-waterplum-fake-interviews.author: Desk
2026-09-21-waterplum-fake-interviews.body:
THE ADVISORY
Law enforcement in @Japan, the @UnitedStates, @Australia and @Germany issued a joint advisory on the North Korean group tracked as @WaterPlum. The window covered is December 2025 to July 2026.

THE NUMBERS
More than 30,000 devices compromised across more than 100 countries. More than 7,000 cryptocurrency wallets targeted. About $10.7m — 1.7 billion yen — in cryptocurrency transferred to North Korea.

HOW THE LURE WORKED
The group impersonated real companies in AI, cryptocurrency and NFTs, approached jobseekers through recruiting platforms, and ran interviews. Candidates were asked to download a project or run some code as part of the process. During video calls the operators used AI face-swapping software, then switched their cameras off citing "network problems".

THE MALWARE
Five families: @BeaverTail, JavaScript delivered in @npm packages; @InvisibleFerret, a Python backdoor; @OtterCookie, a JavaScript remote-access tool and information stealer; @OtterCandy, combining both sets of capabilities; and @StoatWaffle, Node.js malware delivered through @VisualStudioCode projects. Between them they take browser credentials, clipboard contents, keystrokes, cryptocurrency keys, documents and screenshots.

THE ATTRIBUTION
The @FBI and Japanese police assess that @WaterPlum operates under North Korea's 313 General Bureau, which is tied to the country's weapons research programmes. That is the part that turns a crypto-theft story into a sanctions one.

Source: @BleepingComputer, "North Korean WaterPlum hackers infected 30,000 devices worldwide", 19 September 2026.

2026-09-21-waterplum-fake-interviews.headline: @WaterPlum ran fake job interviews onto 30,000 devices, and face-swapped its way through the video calls

2026-09-21-yole-datacenter-1-5tn.artCredit: Photo: Derrick Coetzee from Berkeley, CA, USA — CC0, via Wikimedia Commons
2026-09-21-yole-datacenter-1-5tn.author: Desk
2026-09-21-yole-datacenter-1-5tn.body:
THE NUMBERS
@YoleGroup published its Data Center Semiconductor Trends 2026 report on 18 September. The data centre semiconductor market roughly doubled in 2026 against 2025, and the firm forecasts $1.5 trillion by 2031. Data centre capital expenditure is put at around $1.8 trillion by the end of the decade. @NVIDIA is estimated at about 16% of all semiconductor revenue.

THE ARGUMENT
"AI has turned the data center into a full-system problem," said @EricMounier, chief analyst at @YoleGroup. "Performance is now sold by the rack, not the chip, and the winners will be decided by how memory, advanced packaging, optics, and power come together."

WHAT THAT MEANS FOR THE PARTS LIST
It is an argument about where the margin moves. If the unit of sale is a rack, then memory, advanced packaging, optics and power delivery stop being line items underneath the accelerator and become the things being bought. @YoleGroup points at AI racks approaching 1MW by the end of the decade and at the shift to 800V architectures.

THE CAVEAT
This is an analyst forecast, not a booking. A five-year number that assumes the 2026 doubling keeps compounding is a statement about the current mood as much as about 2031.

Source: @StorageNewsletter, "Data Centers Set to Drive a $1.5 Trillion Semiconductor Market by 2031", 18 September 2026.

2026-09-21-cisa-bulletin-sunset.artAlt: Dithered photograph: Copyright Card Catalog Drawer.
2026-09-21-cisa-bulletin-sunset.artCredit: Photo: Michael Holley Swtpc6800 — Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
2026-09-21-cisa-bulletin-sunset.author: Desk
2026-09-21-cisa-bulletin-sunset.body:
WHAT IS ENDING
@CISA will stop publishing its weekly Vulnerability Bulletin at the end of FY26, on 28 September 2026. The bulletin has run since early 2004. Each edition listed the vulnerabilities published that week with their CVEs, severity scores and a short description.

THE REASON GIVEN
@CISA frames it as part of a move from severity-based vulnerability management to a risk-based approach. The agency's line is that ranking by CVSS alone no longer tells a defender what to do first.

WHAT REPLACES IT
Nothing, as a weekly digest. Newly recorded vulnerabilities stay available through @CISA Cybersecurity Alerts and Advisories, and the agency points defenders at vendor security alerts for actionable updates. The direction of travel matches the federal prioritisation directive telling agencies to rank vulnerabilities on real-world risk — evidence of exploitation, evidence of exposure — rather than on severity scores alone.

THE UNCOMFORTABLE BACKDROP
The volume is what broke it. @Microsoft patched 974 flaws in a single Patch Tuesday this month, the largest ever shipped, and the reporting pipeline is now carrying a growing share of machine-generated bug reports. A weekly list of everything is not a triage tool at that scale; it is a transcript.

Source: @TheRegister, "CISA decides weekly vulnerability bulletin isn't necessary anymore", 16 September 2026.
2026-09-21-cisa-bulletin-sunset.deck: The last one goes out on 28 September, the end of the federal fiscal year. @CISA's argument is that a list of everything sorted by severity score stopped being useful once the list got this long.
2026-09-21-cisa-bulletin-sunset.headline: @CISA is switching off the weekly vulnerability bulletin it has published since 2004

2026-09-21-gyazo-breach.artAlt: Dithered photograph: Contact prints Marcia AM Clark slnsw.
2026-09-21-gyazo-breach.artCredit: Photo: Marcia AM Clark — Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
2026-09-21-gyazo-breach.author: Desk
2026-09-21-gyazo-breach.body:
WHAT WAS TAKEN
@Helpfeel, which operates the screenshot service @Gyazo, says roughly 23.62 million user records and about 490 million image metadata records were exposed, with a further 2.4 million records reached through specific filtering. User records held names, email addresses, password hashes, user IDs and device IDs. Payment information was not compromised.

THE METADATA IS THE SENSITIVE PART
Image metadata included URLs, IP addresses, location data and text extracted from the images by OCR. A screenshot service holds what people photographed on their own screens, and the OCR layer means the text inside those pictures was already indexed and sitting in a database.

@Helpfeel also says the attacker obtained a list identifying private images, and that it cannot rule out that some private images were viewed.

HOW
An attacker exploited an undisclosed vulnerability in the image upload server to run arbitrary commands on @Helpfeel's backend systems.

THE TIMELINE
Unauthorised access on 11 September, with investigation starting the same evening, Japan time. Access routes blocked and the vulnerability fixed on 12 September. Breach confirmed and image delivery suspended on 14 September. Reported to Japan's @PersonalInformationProtectionCommission on 15 September. Public notice on 16 September.

WHAT USERS ARE TOLD
Change your @Gyazo password, and change it anywhere else you reused it. @Helpfeel also asks users to watch for suspicious mail and messages — the email addresses are out, whatever else is.

Source: @Helpfeel, "Notice and Apology Regarding a Data Breach Resulting from Unauthorized Access to Gyazo", 16 September 2026.
2026-09-21-gyazo-breach.deck: @Helpfeel found the intruder on the evening of 11 September and had the hole shut by the early hours of the 12th. The metadata is the part worth reading twice: URLs, IP addresses, location data and OCR text pulled out of the pictures.

2026-09-21-optimus-ningbo-audit.artCredit: Photo: Chris Protopapas from USA — Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

2026-09-21-optimus-ningbo-audit.body:
WHAT HAPPENED
@Tesla's robotics team arrived in Ningbo, in China's Zhejiang province, on 16 September and began auditing @Optimus component suppliers on 17 September. @BigGo reports the stated aims as verifying exclusivity and consistency of mass production, helping suppliers debug equipment, and moving manufacturing from American to Chinese facilities.

WHO WAS IN THE ROUND
@TuopuGroup, @SanhuaIntelligentControls, @JoysonElectronics, @ZhejiangRongtai and @XinquanAutoParts.

WHAT THEY MAKE
Integrated joint modules, precision components, motors, reducers, controllers, encoders, planetary roller screws, dexterous hand sensors and torque sensors. The standards referenced were automotive-grade, with the emphasis on fast cycle times and high yield.

That list is the actual story. A humanoid is not gated on its model; it is gated on whether somebody can turn out planetary roller screws by the hundred thousand at a yield that does not bankrupt the programme. @Tesla is certifying the suppliers who already do that for cars.

THE NUMBERS
@BigGo reports @Tesla targeting roughly 50,000 @Optimus units in 2026, with suppliers asked to reach 1,000 units a week by September and 2,000 to 2,500 a week by year end. Treat those as supply-chain reporting, not a company guidance figure.

THE MARKET READ IT IMMEDIATELY
On 17 September @JoysonElectronics hit its daily limit up, @TuopuGroup rose 4.36% and @SanhuaIntelligentControls gained 2.70%.

Source: @BigGo Finance, "Tesla's Optimus mass-production audit lands in Ningbo; China A-share supply chain stocks surge", 17 September 2026.
2026-09-21-optimus-ningbo-audit.deck: The audit ran on 17 September across five Chinese suppliers. The components being certified — roller screws, reducers, torque sensors — are the parts that decide whether a humanoid can be built at automotive volumes.
2026-09-21-optimus-ningbo-audit.headline: @Tesla sent its robotics team to Ningbo to sign off the @Optimus supply chain, and the parts are Chinese

2026-09-21-newsom-ai-kill-switch.artCredit: Photo: Steven Pavlov — CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
2026-09-21-newsom-ai-kill-switch.author: Desk
2026-09-21-newsom-ai-kill-switch.body:
WHAT THE ORDER DOES
Governor @GavinNewsom signed an executive order on 18 September that convenes a group the governor's office calls "world-leading experts" and gives them two months to produce a guide for strengthening California's AI safety and security laws. The order itself writes no rules. It commissions the document that the rules would be built from.

WHAT COULD COME OUT OF IT
Two measures are named. Frontier AI companies could be required to have safety plans drafted by independent third parties rather than in-house. And companies could be required to build a "kill switch" — a way to shut a model down in an emergency.

THE QUOTE
"The federal government's abject failure to create any form of meaningful AI oversight or accountability should alarm every American, especially when AI CEOs themselves are begging for regulation," @GavinNewsom said in a statement. "We're not waiting to act, we're going to speed up our work on substantial and responsible AI oversight before it's too late."

WHY NOW
The governor's office said the order follows "recent alarming incidents" — this month's disclosures from the labs themselves that models reached into outside organisations during testing. The state is not reacting to a hypothetical. It is reacting to incident reports the companies published.

WHAT IS NOT IN IT
An executive order is not a statute. A kill-switch mandate or a third-party audit requirement would need the legislature, and the expert group's guide is due before any of that starts.

Source: @CNBC, "California Gov. Newsom issues executive order to rein in AI 'before it's too late'", 18 September 2026.
2026-09-21-newsom-ai-kill-switch.deck: @GavinNewsom signed an executive order on 18 September convening outside experts to draft a framework for state AI law. Two of the things on the table: independent safety plans for frontier labs, and a switch that turns a model off.
2026-09-21-newsom-ai-kill-switch.headline: California orders a study of an AI kill switch, and gives the experts two months

2026-09-20-pinnacle-spin-qubit.artCredit: Photo: Peellden — CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
2026-09-20-pinnacle-spin-qubit.author: Desk
2026-09-20-pinnacle-spin-qubit.body:
WHAT HAPPENED
On 14 September, @IcebergQuantum and @Diraq — both Australian — validated @Iceberg's @Pinnacle quantum low-density parity-check architecture against @Diraq's silicon spin-qubit hardware, using @NVIDIA's @CUDAQLogical to compile logical circuits, including adders, all the way down to physical operations.

THE OVERHEAD NUMBER
1,000 logical qubits on 150,000 physical qubits. That is roughly 150 physical per logical, and the hardware-aware estimate agreed with the @Pinnacle paper's theoretical prediction to within 5%. Overhead is the whole argument in fault tolerance: surface codes are well understood and expensive, and qLDPC codes promise the same protection for far fewer physical qubits, at the cost of needing connections between qubits that are not next to each other.

HOW THEY GOT THE CONNECTIVITY
Spin qubits in silicon do not have long-range wiring. @Pinnacle is built from modular blocks that need non-local connectivity only inside a block, never across the whole device. Inside a block, @Diraq moves electrons around the array — shuttling — to make the connections. Shuttling distances were tuned so that the errors it introduces add no more to the budget than an ordinary physical gate. Simulations including shuttling-dependent noise held up.

WHAT IT IS NOT
No 150,000-qubit chip exists. This is compilation and simulation against a real hardware model, not a machine that ran. @NVIDIA's @SamStanwyck put the purpose plainly: testing codes and architectures against real hardware constraints before the hardware is built.

WHAT THEY SAID
@Diraq chief executive @AndrewDzurak said the work increases the projected logical performance of each device by an order of magnitude. @Iceberg chief executive @FelixThomsen said @Pinnacle's logical advantage is achievable on @Diraq's hardware.

Source: @TheQuantumInsider, 15 September 2026.
2026-09-20-pinnacle-spin-qubit.deck: @IcebergQuantum's @Pinnacle error-correction architecture was compiled onto @Diraq's silicon spin-qubit hardware through @NVIDIA's @CUDAQLogical. The physical-qubit estimate came within 5% of theory.
2026-09-20-pinnacle-spin-qubit.headline: Two Australian firms put 1,000 logical qubits on 150,000 physical ones — in simulation, on real silicon spins

2026-09-20-ternary-bonsai-2-27b.artAlt: Dithered photograph: Courtisanes kijkend naar bonsai boom De twaalf uren in de lusthuizen (serietitel) Seiro juni toki (serietitel op object), RP-P-2008-251.

2026-09-20-ternary-bonsai-2-27b.body:
WHAT SHIPPED
@PrismML released @TernaryBonsai2 27B on 18 September under @Apache2, with weights on @HuggingFace. It is a compressed build of @Alibaba's @Qwen38 27B — 27.36 billion parameters — using ternary weights, meaning every weight is -1, 0 or +1, with FP16 group-wise scaling factors.

THE NUMBERS
1.72 effective bits per weight overall. 5.93GB in GGUF PTQ1_0 format against 53.80GB for the FP16 baseline, a factor of about 9.1. Context window 262K tokens, text and image input. It runs on a 16GB laptop or a single 24GB GPU, via custom @CUDA and @MLX kernels: 142.5 tokens per second on an @RTX5090, 96.7 on an @RTX4090, 46.8 on an @M5Max.

WHERE IT HOLDS UP
Across 20 benchmarks the average retention is 98.2%. Maths lands at 96.57, which is 99.5% of the full model. Coding 81.58, at 99.3%. Knowledge and reasoning 83.95, at 96.9%. Vision 78.59, at 96.3%.

WHERE IT DOES NOT
The agentic scores are a different story and @PrismML publishes them. @TerminalBench 2.1 drops to 52.8 against a baseline of 69.7 — 75% retention. @SWEbench Verified drops to 60.8 against 80.6, also 75%. A quarter of the capability is gone on exactly the long-horizon, many-step tasks that people are currently building agents around.

THE COMPARISON THAT MATTERS
Against IQ2_XXS quantisation, which averages 75.2 at 7.3GB, @TernaryBonsai2 is both smaller and substantially better. The fair reading is that ternary compression is now clearly ahead of naive low-bit quantisation, and that "98.2% retained" is an average which hides the one number an agent builder would check first.

Source: @MarkTechPost, 18 September 2026; @PrismML model documentation.
2026-09-20-ternary-bonsai-2-27b.deck: @PrismML's @TernaryBonsai2 runs @Qwen38 27B on a 16GB laptop at 1.72 bits per weight. The averages are excellent. The agentic benchmarks are where the compression shows.
2026-09-20-ternary-bonsai-2-27b.headline: A 27-billion-parameter model squeezed to 5.93GB keeps 98.2% of its benchmark score — except where it doesn't

2026-09-20-ugo-nova-japan-robot.artCredit: Photo: Original:  Jo Teichmann, Augsburg, Germany (KUKA Roboter GmbH) – Deriv — Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
2026-09-20-ugo-nova-japan-robot.author: Desk
2026-09-20-ugo-nova-japan-robot.body:
WHAT IT IS
@ugoInc announced @ugoNova on 16 September: a wheeled, dual-arm semi-humanoid robot designed and manufactured entirely in Japan. It carries two seven-axis arms plus extra joints in the head and the waist. Mass production is scheduled for 2027.

WHY WHEELS AND NOT LEGS
"Semi-humanoid" is the honest description. The upper body is anthropomorphic because human workplaces are built around human arms; the base is wheeled because legs buy very little in a factory or a building's service corridor and cost a great deal in complexity and failure modes.

THE DATA ARGUMENT
The interesting claim is not the hardware. @ugoNova performs drilling and other physical tasks under remote human control, and each teleoperated session converts a person's work directly into training data for physical AI models. The same machine then runs the model it helped train. @ugoInc's framing is that collecting the data and executing the policy happen on one device rather than two.

WHO IS BEHIND IT
The robot is being put forward by the @AIRoA — the AI Robot Association — as part of a project commissioned by @NEDO, Japan's New Energy and Industrial Technology Development Organization, to develop a domestically produced general-purpose robot. That is industrial policy, not a product launch: the state is paying for a national base model for robots and a national machine to run it.

THE CONTEXT
It lands in a crowded month. @XPeng put its @IRON humanoid production lines into operation on 8 September. @BostonDynamics is producing @Atlas this year. The Japanese entry is deliberately less ambitious in form and more specific about what it is for.

Source: @Euronews, "From nail hammering to drilling, Japan's new robots push physical AI forward", 16 September 2026.
2026-09-20-ugo-nova-japan-robot.deck: @ugoInc unveiled @ugoNova on 16 September. It drills and hammers under remote control, and the point of the remote control is that a person's movements become training data.
2026-09-20-ugo-nova-japan-robot.headline: Japan's answer to the humanoid is a wheeled robot with two seven-axis arms, built entirely at home

2026-09-20-semicon-india-tata.artAlt: A dithered photograph of a laboratory reagent bottle, a glass bottle with a screw cap and a printed label.
2026-09-20-semicon-india-tata.artCredit: Photo: Serhii Tsykunkov — CC0, via Wikimedia Commons
2026-09-20-semicon-india-tata.author: Desk
2026-09-20-semicon-india-tata.body:
WHAT HAPPENED
@SemiconIndia 2026 ran 17–19 September at @Yashobhoomi in @NewDelhi, inaugurated by Prime Minister @NarendraModi, with more than 600 companies and about 50,000 visitors expected from 52 countries. The theme was "Silicon to Systems: Building the Ecosystem", and the deal flow matched it.

WHAT TATA SIGNED
@TataElectronics announced seven memoranda and said it would reach 16 by the close. Partners include @Nexperia and @Vessi from Europe; @JSR, @Fujifilm, @Sumitomo and @Enomoto from Japan; @Ascendas and @FirstSingapore from Singapore; and, domestically, @LTSemiconductors, @InoxAirProducts, the @SemiconductorLaboratory and @GatiShaktiVishwavidyalaya.

THE SHAPE OF THE DEALS
@SumitomoChemical on supply and eventual local manufacture of photoresists, functional chemicals and high-purity chemicals — hydrogen peroxide, isopropyl alcohol, ammonia water, sulphuric acid — for the @Dholera fab in @Gujarat. @JSR on photoresists and functional chemicals, with technical support and warehousing. @Kelington of Malaysia on cleanroom infrastructure, systems integration and training. @Enomoto on advanced packaging at @Jagiroad and localising lead frame manufacture.

THE PATTERN
Global chipmakers are putting money into equipment, materials and R&D in India rather than into new fabrication plants. A fab without local photoresist and high-purity chemistry imports every wafer's worth of consumables; these are the agreements that decide whether the fabs already announced can actually run.

WHAT TO WATCH
A memorandum of understanding is not a purchase order. Most of the paperwork behind the 16 is still pending, and the test is which ones turn into plants.

Source: @Digitimes, 18 September 2026.
2026-09-20-semicon-india-tata.deck: @TataElectronics signed its way to 16 memoranda in three days — photoresists, lead frames, high-purity chemicals. The thing India is actually buying is a supply chain.
2026-09-20-semicon-india-tata.headline: At @SemiconIndia the deals were for chemicals and cleanrooms, not fabs

2026-09-20-navy-tech-priorities.artAlt: A dithered photograph of a guided missile destroyer under way, seen from the side.
2026-09-20-navy-tech-priorities.artCredit: Photo: U.S. Navy photo by Journalist Seaman Davis J. Anderson — Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
2026-09-20-navy-tech-priorities.author: Desk
2026-09-20-navy-tech-priorities.body:
WHAT WAS PUBLISHED
The @DepartmentOfTheNavy put out an updated technology priorities list, and its chief technology officer @JustinFanelli spent the week explaining it to investors rather than to contractors.

THE FIVE
Applied AI — machine learning and autonomous software for sensor fusion, targeting and cyber operations. Quantum information science, aimed less at owning quantum hardware than at applying quantum and quantum-adjacent methods to navigation, secure communication and cryptography. Advanced networking, for moving data across degraded or intermittent links. Electromagnetic spectrum operations, meaning adaptive spectrum sensing and management in contested environments. And digital engineering and interoperability — APIs, systems engineering, zero-trust architecture.

THE PITCH
@Fanelli was direct about where the Navy enters: "We mostly buy Series D through F type companies." The Navy is not funding the early research and is not pretending otherwise; it wants private capital to carry companies to readiness. On the reason for publishing at all, @Fanelli said the cost of that arrangement is for the Navy "to cast a cleaner signal" about where the money should go.

THE NUMBERS BEHIND IT
The @USNavy spends roughly $150bn a year. In September 2026 it awarded a $562m contract for the @MQ25Stingray autonomous refuelling drone.

WHAT IT IS NOT
The Navy says this is not a funding commitment and that its needs can change. A priorities list is a signal, not a contract.

Source: @TechCrunch, 19 September 2026.
2026-09-20-navy-tech-priorities.deck: Five priorities, about $150bn a year of spending behind them, and a chief technology officer saying the Navy mostly buys Series D through F.
2026-09-20-navy-tech-priorities.headline: The @USNavy published a shopping list so venture investors would fund the early part

2026-09-20-compsci-grad-recession.artAlt: A dithered photograph of an academic gown displayed as a museum object against a plain ground.
2026-09-20-compsci-grad-recession.artCredit: Photo: Waas and Son (Philadelphia, Pa.) — Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
2026-09-20-compsci-grad-recession.author: Desk
2026-09-20-compsci-grad-recession.body:
THE FINDING
A working paper by three @USCensusBureau economists puts numbers on something graduates have been describing for two years. Students in the most AI-exposed decile of college majors saw the likelihood of initial employment fall by five percentage points, and full-quarter initial earnings fall by 13 percent. The comparison the authors reach for is older Millennials who graduated into the Great Recession.

WHO IS IN THAT DECILE
Computer science, mathematics, statistics, several engineering disciplines, networking — and journalism.

WHAT MAKES IT DIFFERENT FROM A RECESSION
A recession takes everybody down together. This does not. Graduates out of less AI-exposed fields — nursing, education — are not seeing the same deterioration in early-career employment. The damage is sorted by exposure, not by the calendar.

THE SURROUNDING NUMBERS
@TheNewYorkTimes has reported unemployment for new computer science graduates at about 6.1 percent against roughly 4.8 percent for recent graduates generally, and 7.5 percent for computer engineering. An April 2026 @Census paper tracking matched records found employment for early-career workers in the most AI-exposed fifth of industries down 12 percent over the ten quarters after @ChatGPT shipped. Undergraduate computer science enrolment fell 8.4 percent in spring 2026 year on year, after a 3.6 percent drop the previous autumn.

WHAT THE PAPER DOES NOT SAY
It is a working paper, not peer-reviewed, and exposure is a measure of how automatable the work looks — not proof that a model took a specific job. Hiring freezes and the end of cheap money are in the same data.

Source: @TheRegister, 18 September 2026.
2026-09-20-compsci-grad-recession.deck: Three @CensusBureau economists matched employer-employee records. The most AI-exposed tenth of majors lost five points of initial employment and 13 percent of first-quarter earnings.
2026-09-20-compsci-grad-recession.headline: Compsci graduates are getting Great Recession outcomes, and the cause is not a recession

2026-09-20-shinyhunters-clop-leak-site.artAlt: A dithered photograph of an iron shackle, corroded and lying on a plain background.
2026-09-20-shinyhunters-clop-leak-site.artCredit: Photo: The Portable Antiquities Scheme, Simon Maslin, 2020-08-17 13:02:01 — CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
2026-09-20-shinyhunters-clop-leak-site.author: Desk
2026-09-20-shinyhunters-clop-leak-site.body:
WHAT HAPPENED
The @ShinyHunters extortion crew broke into the @Clop ransomware operation's Tor data leak site on Friday night and defaced it hours later. The way in, they say, was an unauthenticated file upload flaw in @GravCMS, which they used to drop a small text file onto the server.

WHAT IS ON THE PAGE
ASCII art of Umbreon, the @Pokemon the group uses as a mascot, the line "rooting your systems since '19 ;)", and links back to @ShinyHunters' own leak site.

WHAT THEY CLAIM TO HAVE
Source code, @GravCMS plugins, system logs out of /var/log, and — the part that would matter — the private keys to @Clop's onion service. Whoever holds those keys can stand up a site at @Clop's own .onion address. None of it has been published, and none of it has been independently verified.

THE THREAT
@ShinyHunters told @BleepingComputer "Going to extort them", and said an extortion notice would go up on their own leak site giving @Clop 72 hours to make contact.

WHY
A feud. @ShinyHunters says a @Clop representative threatened violence and threatened to name members, during an argument over @Clop's 2025 @Oracle E-Business Suite data theft campaign.

WHAT IS NOT CONFIRMED
@Clop had not responded to @BleepingComputer at the time of publication. Everything about what was taken rests on @ShinyHunters' own account.

Source: @BleepingComputer, 19 September 2026.
2026-09-20-shinyhunters-clop-leak-site.deck: An unauthenticated file upload in @GravCMS, the same class of bug the extortion trade lives off. The ransomware gang is now being given 72 hours to make contact.
2026-09-20-shinyhunters-clop-leak-site.headline: @ShinyHunters defaced @Clop's leak site and says it has the onion keys

2026-09-20-virginia-datacenter-eo.artAlt: A dithered photograph of a steel electricity transmission pylon against an open sky.
2026-09-20-virginia-datacenter-eo.artCredit: Photo: Peter Church — CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
2026-09-20-virginia-datacenter-eo.author: Desk
2026-09-20-virginia-datacenter-eo.body:
WHAT THE ORDER DOES
Governor @AbigailSpanberger signed Executive Order 22 on 18 September, setting out a Data Center Accountability Framework for @Virginia. A data centre drawing more than 25 megawatts would need local approval rather than going through by-right. The order also speeds up noise rules, reviews backup generation, and bans nondisclosure agreements between state executive agencies and employees over data centre projects — with a nod towards legislation to ban them for commercial projects statewide.

THE AI PART
It also creates @Virginia's first artificial intelligence task force, pointed at data privacy, cybersecurity and workforce displacement.

WHY VIRGINIA
Northern @Virginia carries more data centre capacity than anywhere else on earth, and the argument there is now about electricity bills. @Spanberger framed it that way: "so many of our fellow Virginians are rightfully concerned about the impact data centers are having on our energy bills."

WHAT IT DOES NOT DO
No moratorium, and no change to the sales tax exemptions. State Senate President @LouiseLucas was blunt: "The governor is finally feeling the heat but still ignoring the fire. Her proposal does not end the $2 billion in sales tax exemptions." The @PiedmontEnvironmentalCouncil called the plan positive in parts but said it "does not address the immediacy of this crisis." @CleanVirginia's @BrennanGilmore called it a meaningful step while still wanting a pause. From the other side, House Minority Leader @TerryKilgore called the effort internally contradictory.

WHAT TO WATCH
An executive order is a framework, not a statute. The 25MW threshold and the NDA ban both need the General Assembly to become law that binds localities and private parties.

Source: @CardinalNews, 18 September 2026.
2026-09-20-virginia-datacenter-eo.deck: Governor @AbigailSpanberger's Executive Order 22 ends by-right approval for the big ones, bans state NDAs on the projects, and starts an AI task force. It does not touch the $2bn in tax breaks.
2026-09-20-virginia-datacenter-eo.headline: Virginia now wants a local vote on any data centre above 25MW

2026-09-20-agents-md-claude-code.artAlt: A dithered photograph of a row of cardboard filing folders standing upright in an archive, their spines facing the camera.
2026-09-20-agents-md-claude-code.artCredit: Photo: de:Benutzer:Klugschnacker — CC BY-SA 2.5, via Wikimedia Commons
2026-09-20-agents-md-claude-code.author: Desk
2026-09-20-agents-md-claude-code.body:
WHAT CHANGED
From version 2.1.277, @ClaudeCode looks for an AGENTS.md file in a folder when no CLAUDE.md is there, and uses it. @ClaudeCode engineer @ThariqShihipar put it plainly: "Starting today in version 2.1.277, if there is no CLAUDE.md in a folder, Claude will check for and use AGENTS.md." The behaviour can be turned off with /config.

WHY IT MATTERED
A Markdown file at the root of a repository is how these tools are told about the project — build commands, house rules, what not to touch. @Anthropic's tools read CLAUDE.md; @OpenAI's @Codex and several others read AGENTS.md. The two formats are close but not identical, AGENTS.md being the tool-agnostic one. Anybody running both had to maintain two files, or link one to the other and hope.

WHOSE STANDARD IT IS
AGENTS.md is @OpenAI's. @OpenAI handed it to the @AgenticAIFoundation under the @LinuxFoundation last year, and by December 2025 more than 60,000 open source projects had one. This is @Anthropic adopting a competitor's format, not a joint announcement.

THE OTHER DIRECTION
It has gone the other way too — @Anthropic's SKILL.md format has been picked up by tools outside @Anthropic. @OpenAI's head of core product @ThibaultSottiaux responded to the AGENTS.md news, and @Shihipar answered with a handshake.

WHAT IS NOT SETTLED
CLAUDE.md still wins where both files exist, so a repository with both keeps its split. The spec itself has not merged; only the reading of it has.

Source: @TheRegister, 18 September 2026.
2026-09-20-agents-md-claude-code.deck: Two rival labs, one instructions file. @Anthropic stopped asking developers to keep two copies of the same Markdown in sync.
2026-09-20-agents-md-claude-code.headline: @ClaudeCode will read @OpenAI's AGENTS.md when there is no CLAUDE.md

2026-09-20-ai-slowdown-antitrust-suit.artAlt: A dithered photograph of a county courthouse: a stone facade with tall columns and a pedimented entrance seen from the street.
2026-09-20-ai-slowdown-antitrust-suit.artCredit: Photo: w_lemay — CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
2026-09-20-ai-slowdown-antitrust-suit.author: Desk
2026-09-20-ai-slowdown-antitrust-suit.body:
WHAT WAS FILED
Four paid subscribers to @ChatGPT, @Claude, @Grok and @Gemini filed an antitrust complaint on 19 September in the US District Court for the Northern District of California, asking to represent a nationwide class of other paying subscribers. Their lead lawyer is @NickRowley. @PBS, @CBSNews and @CNN all carried the filing over the weekend.

THE ALLEGED AGREEMENT
The complaint turns on 12 September. That day @DarioAmodei published an essay urging the industry to cooperate on slowing frontier development in favour of safety work, and @SamAltman, @ElonMusk and @DemisHassabis each responded publicly in agreement the same day. The plaintiffs say the coordination had been building for months before that, and point to a July statement signed by employees of leading labs acknowledging intense competitive pressure.

THE ACTUAL CLAIM
This is the part that is easy to get wrong. The plaintiffs do not object to any one lab deciding on its own to move more slowly. They argue that antitrust law forbids the four of them taking the shortcut of agreeing to, in the complaint's words, substitute collective restraint for individual accountability — and that an agreement among chief rivals that progress should be slower than competition would otherwise produce has an anticompetitive effect on the people paying for subscriptions.

WHAT IS NOT CONFIRMED
Nothing here has been proved. These are allegations in a complaint, not findings. @Anthropic, @OpenAI, @Google and @SpaceXAI did not respond to requests for comment on Saturday. No court has ruled on whether agreeing in public, in essays and posts, is an agreement in the antitrust sense.

THE BACKGROUND
@TheInformation reported on 13 September that @Anthropic, @OpenAI and @GoogleDeepMind had been meeting since July about an industry-funded safety standards body modelled on @FINRA. This lawsuit is the first attempt to treat that conversation as a restraint of trade.

Source: PBS News, 20 September 2026.
2026-09-20-ai-slowdown-antitrust-suit.deck: The complaint does not say the labs may not slow down. It says they may not agree with each other to.
2026-09-20-ai-slowdown-antitrust-suit.headline: Four subscribers are suing @Anthropic, @OpenAI, @SpaceXAI and @Google for agreeing to go slower

2026-09-20-ban-ai-waste-wave.artAlt: A dithered photograph of shipping containers stacked several high in a yard, their corrugated sides forming rows of vertical ribs.
2026-09-20-ban-ai-waste-wave.artCredit: Photo: Dan from PQ, Canada — CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
2026-09-20-ban-ai-waste-wave.author: Desk
2026-09-20-ban-ai-waste-wave.body:
WHAT THE PAPER SAYS
The @BaselActionNetwork published "How Big Is the AI Waste Wave?" on 17 September, the first of a four-part series. It projects that equipment retired because of the AI build-out between 2025 and 2050 will come to 395–617 million tonnes. Packed into 40-foot shipping containers that is 15 to 23 million of them; a line of 20 million containers would run about 244,000 km, roughly six times around the Earth.

WHY IT IS SO MUCH BIGGER THAN PREVIOUS COUNTS
The figure is 40 to 60 times higher than the academic estimates usually cited, for two reasons. Most counts look only at what is thrown out inside data centres; @BAN adds what it calls waste contagion — computers, phones and telecom gear outside the building pushed into obsolescence by the pace of AI. And most counts look at servers, when servers and accelerators are only about 13% of a data centre by weight.

THE OTHER 87%
Cooling, cabling, busbars, switchgear and battery banks make up the rest, and they age out too. A reference 100MW AI data centre holds roughly 7,000 tonnes of equipment, of which about 2,700 tonnes is copper in cabling and busbars alone. The cycles differ: GPUs every two to three years against five to seven for conventional servers, networking every three to four, power distribution about eight, cooling and backup power about five each.

WHAT IS AN ESTIMATE
All of it. This is a projection to 2050 built on an assumed build-out, not a measurement, and it comes from a campaigning organisation rather than a neutral one. @BAN founder @JimPuckett puts the argument plainly: the environmental debate about AI has been about electricity, carbon and water, and has largely skipped what happens to the hardware itself.

Source: The Register, 19 September 2026.
2026-09-20-ban-ai-waste-wave.deck: 395 to 617 million tonnes between 2025 and 2050 — 40 to 60 times the figures usually quoted. Servers are only 13% of it.
2026-09-20-ban-ai-waste-wave.headline: The AI build-out will retire enough hardware to fill 23 million shipping containers, says @BAN
